title: Travel document checklist: verify each traveler
dek: Check passports, entry permissions, children's paperwork and booking names, then record who carries each original and where the backups are kept.
metaDescription: Check passports, entry permissions, children's paperwork and booking names, then record who carries each original and where the backups are kept.

paragraphs: For an international trip, check each traveler's passport, destination and transit permissions, booking names and any child-specific documents. Record the rule you checked, its official source and who carries the original. A passport photo helps with reference information; it does not replace the required document.

One person can have every ticket saved while another person's passport is still in a drawer. The useful checklist is therefore per traveler, not simply 'passports packed.' This guide is for US citizens preparing an international air trip. Other nationalities and land or sea travel may need different checks.

body.heading: Verify before making inflexible bookings
items: Open every traveler's passport and record its exact name, expiry and relevant condition.
Check the destination's official entry requirements and the State Department country information.
Check transit points, return travel and any relevant residency or dual-nationality requirements.
Verify visa or electronic authorization needs through official channels and track application status.
Confirm child documentation, custody-related requirements and consent needs with the relevant authorities.
Compare booking names with the travel documents and ask the carrier about any discrepancy.
Record the date checked and repeat the review before departure.

body.heading: Do not use a universal validity rule
paragraphs: Some destinations require passport validity beyond the visit, and rules may also address blank pages or particular passport types. Write the actual requirement for your route instead of assuming 'six months everywhere.' Check the relevant government's instructions and ask the carrier about boarding requirements if the position is unclear.

The [State Department international checklist](https://travel.state.gov/en/international-travel/planning/checklist.html) points travelers toward destination research, required documents and insurance. Processing times and authorization systems change. Use current official information rather than a fixed renewal timeline copied from an old article.

body.heading: Invented example: one family's document record
rows: Embassy guidance reviewed; needed documents obtained
Offline copy plus separate paper record

body.heading: Children need a separate check
paragraphs: Do not assume an adult's documents cover an accompanying child. [USAGov](https://www.usa.gov/travel-documents-children) explains that consent letters may be needed when a child travels alone or with one parent, and directs families to the destination embassy or consulate for entry and exit requirements.

A consent letter is not a universal substitute for custody orders or other required evidence. Where family circumstances are disputed or an order restricts travel, get appropriate legal guidance. Confirm any airline rules for an unaccompanied minor directly with that airline.

body.heading: Separate originals, useful copies and private data
paragraphs: Keep required originals accessible during the journey, not in a checked bag that may be unavailable at the desk. Make secure copies and keep a backup separate from the originals. Avoid posting passport numbers and full document scans in a broad group chat.

For each item, write who carries it and its location. A shared checklist can say 'passport verified; carried by Avery' without exposing all identifiers. Booking references may also allow access to personal trip details, so share them deliberately.

body.heading: Add the records that solve a desk problem
paragraphs: Keep flight and lodging confirmations, onward arrangements where relevant, insurance details and assistance contacts findable offline. Check destination rules for medicines and supporting documentation through official guidance; do not assume original packaging alone makes every medicine lawful to carry.

For domestic travel, use the current authority and carrier instructions rather than transferring international rules. This page does not list every accepted domestic ID or alternative process. For paper records that support the trip, see [what to keep on paper](/guides/what-to-keep-on-paper-when-you-travel).

body.heading: Stop if eligibility is unresolved
paragraphs: An authorization still pending, damaged passport, name mismatch or unclear entry rule is not a box to tick optimistically. Contact the issuing authority, destination officials or carrier as appropriate before departure. Do not treat an agent's informal reassurance as a substitute for an official requirement.

If a required passport is lost abroad, use [the lost-passport preparation guide](/guides/lost-passport-wallet-or-phone-abroad-what-to-have-ready). Preserve copies and reference details, but follow the actual replacement process rather than expecting a scan to board you.

items.q: Does every passport need six months left?
items.a: No universal six-month rule applies to every international route. Requirements depend on destination, nationality, passport type and sometimes transit or residence status. Check official information for your actual journey and record the rule beside the expiry date rather than relying on the expiry alone.

items.q: Should one adult carry all the documents?
items.a: Assign responsibility deliberately and tell the relevant travelers where their documents are. Consider separation, access and the risk of losing one folder. There is no single best arrangement for every group; the important thing is knowing who has each original when it is needed.

items.q: Is a consent letter always mandatory for a child?
items.a: Requirements vary by country, travel arrangement and family circumstances. USAGov says such letters may be needed and recommends checking with the destination embassy or consulate. Ask about language, notarization and any additional evidence rather than assuming a generic letter meets all requirements.
